Box 83720 Boise, ID 83720-0038 S ubmitted via email: chanel.tewalt@isda.idaho.gov, jraymond@house.idaho.gov and tnichols@senate.idaho.gov RE: B io security lap ses at Idaho do mestic elk farms Dear Director Tewalt, Senator Nichols and Representative Raymond, Idaho’s native deer, elk, and moose are central to our identity—feeding our families, supporting rural economies, and connecting Idahoans to the landscapes we call home. But a disturbing pattern of biosecurity lapses at domestic elk operations is increasing the risk of Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) spreading to Idaho’s native wildlife and forcing costly responses that Idaho’s hunters, wildlife managers and citizens should not have to shoulder. In late 2024 and early 2025, the first two confirmed CWD detections in domestic elk were reported in eastern Idaho. Only a year earlier, ISDA had approved imports of source animals 1

# Page 2^page=2
from facilities in Alberta, Canada, near a known CWD hotspot - introducing an avoidable and unnecessary risk to both domestic and wild cervids. In the same period, Idaho removed double-fence requirements for domestic elk facilities and expanded flexibility for operators to move quarantined elk into high fence hunt enclosures - many of which border public lands in prime deer, elk and moose habitat. The Idaho Conservation League (ICL) and many other stakeholders opposed such measures in public testimony, stating that reduced biosecurity measures would increase CWD risk to wild herds and push more obligations onto hunters and IDFG. To day, so cial media chan n els fo r ID FG, KIVI, KTVB an d o thers are buzzin g after ID FG issued a p ress release (2/12/26) co n firmin g that the agen cy was fo rced to lethally remo ve o ver 80 deer that had accessed an elk farm en clo sure n o rth o f Rexburg due to C WD co n cern s. Ingress of wild cervids was enabled by apparent biosecurity lapses of operators. While o n lin e feedback is n ever scien tific, the 1000+ weeken d reactio n s do sho w the issue immediately disturbed sp o rtsmen an d the gen eral p ublic. Those sentiments were further inflamed after IDFG disclosed that IDFG and ISDA had paid for meat processing - not the owners of the facility. Public records from ISDA and IDFG document several other repeated containment failures at domestic cervid facilities in 2025. Additionally, recent instances of other biosecurity breaches and/or positive CWD tests illustrate the pattern that has persisted for many years (see timelin e highlights o n P. 5). These troubling incidents are not merely operational lapses—they undermine Idaho’s responsibilities to Public Trust beneficiaries. Section 204, Subsection 04 of 02.04.19 (Rules Governing Domestic Cervidae) says that “the A dministrator may effectuate the capture of the escaped domestic cervidae to ensure the health o f Idaho ’s livesto ck an d wild cervidae p o p ulatio n s.” In this passage, the State of Idaho plainly acknowledges that without strict adherence to prudent biosecurity protocols, domestic cervids pose a threat to livestock and wild cervids. Accordingly, this year, IDFG added GMU 63A to its list of mandatory CWD sampling locations - the first such req uiremen t made fo r hun ters in the eastern half o f the state. This man agemen t actio n was o n ly n ecessitated by the p resen ce o f C WD at do mestic elk ran ches in the area. Subsequent additional CWD detections in the area have prompted IDFG to now consider expansion of mandatory check stations into adjacent GMUs, such as Unit 69. The ICL is also concerned that public records from ISDA and IDFG show that basic requirements set forth in HB 591, as well as longstanding ISDA rules governing domestic cervid operations, are not being followed by several operators. IDFG’s news release of the removal effort near Rexburg has only served to deepen the public’s concerns about the ability of both agencies to address disease threats from domestic elk farms. 2

Whether it’s quarantined animals that escape elk farms and mix with wild deer, elk and moose, hunters being forced to stop at new CWD check stations, or agencies paying the costs to cull and butcher wild animals after they’ve accessed quarantined elk farms, the State is literally asking sportsmen and Idaho’s public to shoulder the collateral damages of domestic elk farms. This is unacceptable. The eviden ce is mo un tin g that do mestic cervid p ro ducers have n o t demo n strated they can o p erate witho ut jeo p ardizin g wildlife reso urces that belo n g to all Idaho an s. The ICL is also troubled that recent modifications to earlier rules governing domestic cervids have only served to increase biosecurity threats. For example, in the case of a domestic bull elk sourced to a Blackfoot facility, earlier standards for 100% testing of domestic elk mortalities (instead of the current 10% requirement) would have given owners a better understanding of their disease risk profile and could likely have prevented transfer of an animal that later tested CWD-positive. We’re also concerned that owners may also have unknowingly sourced infected elk to other parts of the state. The IC L urges ISD A to rigo ro usly in vestigate all recen t in ciden ts described here an d imp lemen t ap p licable admin istrative actio n s an d/o r reco mmen d civil p en alties sho uld vio latio n s be p ro ven . The IC L also resp ectfully en co urages the Idaho legislature to take actio n s to revisit HB 591 an d stren gthen testin g req uiremen ts, bio security measures an d en fo rcemen t mechan isms fo r Idaho ’s do mestic cervid o p eratio n s. The ICL has developed a comprehensive set of recommendations for ISDA and IDFG and looks forward to working through proper channels, including both legislative chambers and diverse stakeholders, to remedy the issues outlined above. Timelin e o f kn o wn p o ten tial vio latio n s regardin g bio security measures ● Dec. 2024 - Jan. 2025: ISDA announced that two domestic elk farms tested positive for CWD, initiating quarantine orders for both operations. ● August 2025: IDFG euthanized a bull moose discovered inside a CWD-quarantined high-fence enclosure; later that season, a domestic bull elk escaped the same facility and was shot on public land nearly three miles away. ● Fall 2025: A domestic bull elk traced to an operation in eastern Idaho was shot on BLM land roughly 16 miles away; weeks later, six wild mule deer were shot by staff and family members inside the enclosure. ● Late 2025: Nearly 10 additional positive CWD cases were found at Idaho facilities. ● Late 2025: A third operation in north Idaho was issued a quarantine notice from ISDA, after owners in Bonners Ferry sourced a bull elk to a Blackfoot high-fence “hunt park” this past fall (over 500 miles away), which later tested positive for CWD. Owners may have unknowingly sourced infected elk to other parts of the state, as well. ● December 2025: IDFG officials documented improper disposal of CWD-exposed domestic elk carcasses at a quarantined operation and were forced to lethally remove a wild cow elk observed in the area. ● Feb. 12, 2026: Per IDFG press release, the agency concluded a lethal deer removal operation north of Rexburg, killing over 80 mule deer found within a 5,400-acre enclosure. 5
